lines: Testing every pair of a thousand segments means testing nearly half a million pairs, most of which never cross.
On eight segments that waste is already visible: twenty-eight pairs, and only two of them actually meet.
Think about what a crossing requires: two segments have to be adjacent in some ordering before they can swap places.
answer: Only a pair that becomes neighbors in that ordering can ever cross, so a sweep only ever has to test those.

lines: Call the coordinates where anything could change events, and call whatever the line currently touches the active set.
Between two consecutive events nothing changes, so the whole algorithm is just: handle the next event, update, move on.
A half-open interval excludes its own right end, so at a shared coordinate the ending interval has to leave first.
Reverse that order and the algorithm briefly believes two intervals that only touch are actually overlapping.
A heap that always hands back the tallest live building needs a way to forget buildings that already ended.
Lazy deletion postpones that forgetting until the stale entry would otherwise be read, instead of removing it immediately.
Every one of those seven points is a moment the tallest building in view changed, nothing more.
A fixed sliding window would use a deque; this window's membership depends on when a building ends, not its position.
A running count only ever answers one question: is anything covered. It cannot say where the coverage changed.
answer: A tree that tracks a cover count per node answers both questions in logarithmic time, which a plain count cannot.

lines: Thirty-four counts every rectangle's area once each, so wherever two rectangles overlap, that strip gets counted twice.
Subtract the double-counted strips and the true union, twenty-nine, is what a vertical sweep recovers without ever drawing the shape.
A segment's left endpoint inserts it into the active set; its right endpoint removes it, same as the depth sweep before it.
A crossing is not known in advance, so the algorithm has to discover it and insert it as a new event.
If two segments were never adjacent in the ordering, there is no way for them to swap places without a third segment moving first.
So testing only newly-adjacent pairs is not a shortcut that might miss something; it is the entire set of ways a crossing can occur.
The whole appeal of this algorithm was spending less work when there are few crossings to report.
answer: Once crossings are as dense as a quadratic number, the extra logarithm in the sweep's cost outweighs that saving entirely.

lines: A thousand segments scattered loosely enough to rarely cross still only produce forty-eight crossings, nowhere near a quadratic count.
The pairs a naive scan tests, though, grow with the square of the segment count regardless of how many actually meet.
Deciding which side of a line a point sits on reduces to the sign of one arithmetic expression, computed once.
That sign is exact when the coordinates are integers, but rounds unpredictably near zero once the coordinates are floating point.
A database join with two inequality conditions faces the same shape of problem this topic just swept through, one layer down.
Sorting each side once and merging the two orders turns a quadratic comparison into something closer to the cost of sorting.
Three different problems, three different active-set structures, and the same two design questions asked of each: what changes, and what structure holds it.
Every bound shown here held for every input; the next milestone's algorithms instead make promises about an average over many random ones.
